learner_facing_text: Entry-level stagehand work commonly spans load-in, performance/show support, load-out and related venue/event tasks, but exact call shape, employer structure and assignment mix vary by production and sector.
notes: Module-level evidence family; lesson-level exact-source backfill remains.

learner_facing_text: A new stagehand should recognize changing hazards, preserve control, report or escalate conditions they do not understand, and avoid improvising a technical fix or operating controlled equipment without the required assignment/training/authorization.
notes: Hazard/risk/behavior is a Crew Blueprint teaching model, not one codified OSHA three-part taxonomy.

learner_facing_text: Work preparation is context-dependent: call instructions, task hazards, employer/site rules and production phase determine required clothing, PPE and readiness; show clothing is not a substitute for hazard-selected PPE.
notes: Detailed exact PPE claims live in content_fundamentals_qualified.jsonl.

learner_facing_text: Before starting work, orient to the actual site, reporting structure, work paths, exits, equipment traffic and changing conditions; recognize controlled work zones and remain a pedestrian/support worker around powered equipment unless separately trained and authorized.
notes: Accessibility/public-event acceptance remains a separate authority layer.

learner_facing_text: Useful entry-level communication means receiving the assignment from the controlling work structure, confirming unclear instructions, reporting problems or completion, and returning through the established lead/steward/department process rather than self-assigning across departments.
notes: Exact phrases and local reporting rules vary; SFS-O02–O04 deepen this pattern.

learner_facing_text: Load-in commonly includes unloading, moving cases/equipment, distributing/staging materials and supporting assembly or cable work under direction; the beginner's transferable responsibility is controlled material flow, clear communication and respecting department/specialist ownership.
notes: Dedicated Field Skills now carry deeper movement/task evidence; Fundamentals should remain the conceptual home.

learner_facing_text: Tool and equipment literacy begins with recognizing the item, checking the call/task requirements and obvious condition, and asking before unfamiliar use; carrying or recognizing a tool does not authorize every task that tool can perform.
notes: Specific powered, cutting, electrical-testing, rigging and overhead tool use remains outside general beginner instruction.

learner_facing_text: Load-out commonly involves strike, packing, movement and reloading for transport. Fatigue, congestion, visibility and schedule pressure can matter, but Crew Blueprint should not present load-out as universally more dangerous than load-in or infer release merely because one task is finished.
notes: SFS-O07/O08 supply the task-done vs department/call-release/timekeeping distinction.

learner_facing_text: Physical support, conceptual understanding, observed practice, employer authorization and specialist qualification are different states; a general stagehand course may teach recognition and boundaries without granting technical or controlled-work authority.
notes: This is both cross-source role evidence and Crew Blueprint's canonical authority-state framework.

learner_facing_text: Stagehands enter and progress through multiple employer, labor-provider, referral/hiring-hall and local training pathways; reliability, punctuality, professionalism, safety and willingness to learn are recurring expectations, but there is no single national callback score or universal 30-day progression model.
notes: Current early-call sequence remains explicitly Crew Blueprint framing.
